A Hexane or • Moll Flanders may indeed be summeaful through the unscrupulouness of their vices for a time, may live and even flourish through the weakness of their 41,110Cilltel and their own wickedness, but a time comes when their sine have found them out, and , the prosperous harlot and the fortunate thief ore reduced to beggary and ruin before ,we shut up the book at the end of the last , chapter. But in a book, the first volume of which is just published, we have none of such con- solation. The career described in it, though hill of mendacious boldness and tricky in- trigue, menu to be still a successful one, and what one would fain believe to be the natural oonaequenoes of the conduct recorded it its pages, the contempt of all , honest men, has not yet followed. True it is that the bookie still incomplete. The author of this book records that a 1 reader of the narrative has declared that 1 after he had primed a certain portion of the I book he was more than ever oonvinced of Mr. Insraeh's life-long consistency. So he may have been, but we take it that that con- sistency was rather that of the far-famed Vicar of Bray than of any other noble and more generous example. When in early , life he thought that itadicaliam wee the most likely means of bringing him before the public he could humbly apply to such men as O'Connell, Joseph flume, and Bur- dett, for certificates of character cud conduct. When he th .ught that dir B. Peel might . help him he became an advocate of Free-Trade, and smarted that the introduo- Ron of ouch • meaaure belonged to the con- servative party. When Peel would hare', none of him in his ministry he showered tor- rents of abuse on him for having, as • teader of the Comervative party, introduced the repeal of the Corn-Laws. Hu was a lift& eel, young Englishman, and Tory in turn, changing over and over again as he thought the temper of the people and hie own interesto beat required, and seems to have taken the greatest delight in throwing dirt on the men' whom he had before moot assiduoualy cour- ted. Of course in the life ef every Statesman times will come when from the changes of cir- cumstances from the awakened conscience of the country, or even from thealtered opinions of the man himself, he is constrained to sup- port what he had before opposed, and to turn his back on some of his once moat cherished convictions; but such changes are usually accompanied by the loss of power, by the desertitm of friends, and by lessened influence. It haa been for Lord Beaconsfield loupe to have the good-fortune that each time he has changed his opinion he has gained a step on the ladder, that each in- ' consistency has benefited him in his career, ' and that he is now Prime Minister of Eng- land, having raised himself to that pitch by the abjuration of every opinion which Wing 911 t 19 b tuccrwooll We ma

aware that Lord Beaconsfield's defends's assert that there is agreement between hie earliest and latest political utterances, and that he hes been consistent throughout in hi. assertion that the Tories are the really democratic party, and that the party was to be saved by dropping Tory and adopting Liberal matinees, but there is this sus- picious circumstance to be found in the his- tory of hie opinions—That whenever it has been convenient to drop such an opinion for thetime it has been dropped, and its re-asser- tion has always taken place at a time when its re-adoption was convenient. Our belief is that the first question which Lord Beeconsfield asks himself is whether it will pay to hold such and such a view, and if he finds it convenient to do so, he then seta to work to find a reason which he may give to the world for holding it; and it would be hard if having at one time or another pro- fessed nearly every shade of political opinions, he could not show himself consis- tent to some extent. We most be excused If, when looking at each instance of changed opinion, when noticing how these changes have led to advancement or to power, we judge Lord Beaconsfield by the ordinary rules which we shall apply to less clever but equally unscrupulous men, and to use his own expreesion, meet him with the" fatooos dilemma of insincerity or apostacy." Men are to be judged by the companions they keep, the eassuples which they admire, and the books which they study. If a thief, brought up for judgment, were to plead his innocence, but it were shown that lie took Dick Turpin for his example, read constantly the Newgate Calendar, sod preferred the company of convicted felons to that of honest men, we think the judge would hardly be- lieve his plea, but sentence him to a heavy punishment, If a woman accused of on. chastity were to be found reading French novels, and admiring the life of the Dame de Camellia's, we doubt whether society would not condemn her unheard; and it strikes us that Mr. Dieraeli has put himself out of court by his professed admiration of Lord Bolingbroke. "An oligarchy is hoitile to genius," writes Mr. Disraeli. "Bolingbroke oppoeed the Whige," "Bolingbroke was a man of genius, and recoiling from Tory tenets, which his energetic and vigorous mind taught him at the same time te dread and contemn. Lord Bolingbroke, at the outset of his career, incurred the common- place imputation of insincerity and incon- stancy, because in an age of unsettled par- ties, with professions contradictory of his conduct, he maintained that vigilant independence which is the privilege of an original and independent spirit:. " Mutato numine de to, Fsbula narrator." It seems to us that in this eulogium on Lord Bolingbroke Mr. Disraeli wen writing his own history, and yet it is of this man that Lord Stanhope, himself a Tory states- man, and father of a member of Lord Beaconsfield's Government, says Re en- tered life endowed with every gift of nature, of fortune, and education, except the most important of all—fixed principle. He utterly wanted virtue. When excluded from political life, there were no intrigues, how- ever low and grovelling, to which he did not stoop in order to return to it." And this is the model which our Premier would fashion himself after. These are the principles he profeeeso himself constant to. To dish the Whigs by adopting, and more than adopt- ing, their policy. To take a leap in the . dark, by forcing hie party to desert all the , • which for years dirty had pro- feesed—thie is the 7:ndut polingbroke would have admired, and such which, to get or to keep power, Lord Beaconsfield his suoceosfully imitated. Mr. Goechen, in a speech made last session, warned us against the lowering of the County Franchise, feariog lest the in- terests of the many might overpower the wisdom and the justice of the few, and lest property and capital should be at the mercy of an unmincipled mob. Were we to be certain of such leaders as Lord Bolingbroke awl his follower and admirer, Lord Beacons- field, for the future, we too should agree with him. It is by such men that the people are alternately cajoled and bullied. It is such men as these who lead the 02851135 to acts of injustice ,• who, laugh- ing at and de: Meing the people in reality, use them merely as tools to keep themselves in place and power, and care little for the prosperity of the country as long as they can provide for their own sycophants by a succession of the most hideous jobs. It is because we have faith in the people, be- cause we believe that, left to themselves, they will choose better leaders, and banish all thoughts of class intermits if thereby the nation wili floursh •, because we know that the love of England is greater in the heart of the English working man than the love of his peculiar order or trade, that we demand that the people shall govern, and deny the benefit' of the eystein advocated by Lord Beitoonefield that the aristocracy shall govern for the people. It is all very well to have a pack of dukes and landed gentlemen in a Cabinet, but such men do not and cannot know the wants of the country, and become merely watchers on Providence, to see how little will satisfy the demands of the con- stituencies, and how best they can substitute shams for realities. There was the IMMO franchiae in the time of Mr. Gladstone's Ministry as there has been since the acces- sion to power of Lord Beaconetield, and yet though the Parliament of 1868 and 1874 were elected by a similar constituency, how different have the measure. been carried. During the first period the measures were thorough and drastic. Class-intorest after tines-interest was abolished, great and exhaustive principles were laid down, no fear or favour was ahewn to special interests. What has been done by the present Parliament under the leadership of Lord Beaconefield 7 Economy has been at a discount, the meddlesome intrusion of Government into matters formerly left to local and induotrial energies has come in vogue ; demagogueism, in the form of sub- servience to intereata of class, and the avoid- awe of unpopular reforms, has been largely practised. Mixed questions have been taken hold of by their popular end, and the unpopular but wholesome part has been left to stand over itne dii. Thus hen been , handled the great subject of Local Govern- ment. The Administration has been in office for four sessions, and has not lifted a hand, except to give away in suecesiive doses of public money administered to the ratepayers, the powerful leverage by which they might have propelled the movement of 1 a greet and truly constitutional reform. Such are Mr. Gladetone's own words, and though he is careful to avoid giving any ' epeeist reason for the decadence in parlia- mentary vigour, beyond a denial that it is due to the adoption of household suffrage, we at least used have no such reticence. We say that it is from the character of its leaders that the conduct of Parliament will be deter- mined. With Mr. Gladstone in power the 'lmperial Parliament, spite of the gradual , preponderance of what he has ventured to call a " gerontocracy and a plutocracy," was I capable of great things. With Lord Beacons- field as Premier, it has degenerated into a selfish vestry, desirous of avoiding all heroic work, preferring permissive to peremptory Rota, and anxious that each interest should get a special advantage for itself, pecuniary or otherwise. But from an English gentleman, and even if possible more irom an Etiglieti Premier, perfect truthfulness is nesesaary. A. man may from circumstances be inconsistent, but at least he can be truthful. Can we by the light which we gain in reading the Life of Lord Beaconsfield say that he has ever hesi- tated to assert what gaited hie purpose,. or to deny what it was convenient to get rid of? Even in his most frank utterances has there not frequently been something which has left the appearance that all has not been loll? He in one speech asserts Wycombe to be hie birthplace. He allowed it to be be- lieved that he was educated at Winchester. lie denies that he was a Eadical, after he had asked the most prominent men of that party to be his sponsors at an election, lie gives the he at Shrewsbury to Mr. Yardley, who produced evidence of his indebtadneaa, amt aute us have the list 01 the judgments the 040.4 1/5141t Rd is Took 110

The training of the attorney's office, short as it was, has left a taint upon him, and he prefers to be smart rather than open. We take it that this is nearly • necessary ad- junct to his position. With no English sympathies of blood and parentage, alien to those whom he is aaaociated with, having gained his position by playing ell the weak- news and flattering the prejudice.) of a totally different clean from his own, he is bound to rule by management and not by symeathy. He must be all things to all men, and it is necessary to keep his position that he should change as those change from time to time with whom he is connected, and yet that somehow those changes shall be vindi- cated. It is not a noble position, but it is a necessary one for one who desires power and place, and intends to get and to keep ouch at all hazards. Prime Ministers have lived and died be- fore Lora Beaoonsfield, and their lives have been written, which is, we suppose, the equivalent for the bhaksperian phrase, "the worms have eaten them." Some have been stupid and honest, some wrong headed, some flippant, some have involved their country in heavy losses, some have conferred 1 great benefits on England, a few, perhaps, [ have boon unscrupulous, and a few corrupt. But we take it this ia the only instance whore, , in the lifetime of a Premier such a biography , has been attempted, and in no other ease (lonia 1 so heavy an indictment Wive been preferred , and so strongly defended by indisputable , proof. It is aa accurate and prosaic as the brief [ of a counsel against a prisoner charged with felony, and like that document it is meant to convince the public of what manner of mania in the dock before them. The question which the reader will have to decide for himself is not whether Lord Beaconsfield is clever; not whether lie can say sharp things; not whether he is an extraordinary, and, in some respects, an almost unique specimen of in- tellectual power; not whether he may not [ hibre been in some eases a fast friend as I well as a it ind hater; not whether his novels and pamphlets are smart and witty; not whether he is a good debater and a power- ful orator ; all this he may be, and yet there may be one thing wanting. From the evidence contained in this book the verdict hoe to be given.
